Maximilien Robespierre. Born in 1758, this man was the architect of the Reign of Terror and the most infamous figure of the French Revolution. A provincial lawyer and idealistic radical, he rose to prominence as a deputy to the Estates-General in 1789 and became a leading voice in the radical Jacobin Club by the early 1790s. He built his power on appeals to virtue, the General Will, and the sovereignty of the people, positioning himself as the revolution's moral conscience against compromise and betrayal. He called for the trial and execution of King Louis XVI in December 1792, arguing that the king's survival threatened the republic. The king was executed in January 1793, a psychological turning point that made terror systematic.

In July 1793, Robespierre was elected to the Committee of Public Safety and quickly became its dominant figure. He expanded the secret police and accelerated mass arrests of suspected counter-revolutionaries. He presided over the Reign of Terror from 1793 to 1794, during which over 16,000 were officially executed and thousands more died in prisons or summary killings. The Terror's reach spread into the provinces through guillotines and mass drownings. He orchestrated the executions of major rivals. Danton and Camille Desmoulins were executed in April 1794 for moderation. Hébert and the ultra-revolutionaries were executed in March 1794 for pushing terror too far. His unpredictable judgment made anyone question whether they might be next. He championed the Festival of the Supreme Being in June 1794, a quasi-religious civic ceremony reflecting his Rousseauian belief in virtue, national rebirth, and the dangers of atheism. It was an eerie cultural moment amid mass killing.

But his paranoia and unpredictability eventually alarmed even his allies. After June 1794, he threatened further purges, making deputies fear they might be next to fall. During the Thermidorian Reaction on July 27 and 28, 1794, the Convention voted to arrest him. He was executed by guillotine the next day without trial, the same year he had risen to power. His final hours involved a failed suicide attempt, shooting himself in the jaw before the guillotine. Robespierre believed absolutely in the revolution's moral mission. He saw enemies everywhere because he believed the stakes were eternal. His idealism made him terrifying, convinced as he was of the righteousness of his cause and able to rationalize the execution of anyone who disagreed with him as a defense of the nation's virtue. He represents the eighteenth century's faith in reason and virtue weaponized into totalitarianism, a cautionary tale about the dangers of revolutionary purity when divorced from democratic accountability.
